questions.problem:
Consider the vector space ${R}_{2}[t]$ of all polynomials in the variable $t$ over $R$ with degrees at most $2.$

Which of the following statements are true?

- ${0,1,t}$ is a linearly independent set in ${R}_{2}[t]$
- $2-t$ can be expressed as a linear combination of ${0,1,t}$
- ${0,1,t}$ is a basis of ${R}_{2}[t]$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Notice that 

$$
1\cdot 0+0\cdot 1+0\cdot t=0,
$$

 
where the first coefficient is nonzero, so the set is linearly dependent. In general, any set that contains a zero-vector is linearly dependent.

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
2-t=0\cdot 0+2\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot t.
$$

- Statement III is false. Since the set is not linearly independent, it can't form a basis.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

Which of the following statements are true?

- ${t,{t}^{2}}$ is a linearly independent set in ${R}_{2}[t]$

- ${t,{t}^{2}}$ is a basis of ${R}_{2}[t]$

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot t+{x}_{2}\cdot {t}^{2}=0,

is true if and only if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0.$ So, the set is linearly independent.

- Statement II is false. Notice that all linear combinations of

$$
{t,{t}^{2}}
$$

result in polynomials without the constant term.

- Statement III is false. Indeed, the polynomial ${t}^{2}+1$ can't be written as a linear combination of the set  ${t,{t}^{2}}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

questions.problem:
Consider the vector space ${R}_{3}[t]$ of all polynomials in the variable $t$ over $R$ with degrees at most $3.$

Which of the following statements are true?

- ${1,t,{t}^{2},{t}^{3}}$ is a linearly independent set in ${R}_{3}[t]$
- ${t}^{3}-3t+8$ can be expressed as a linear combination of ${1,t,{t}^{2},{t}^{3}}$
- ${1,t,{t}^{2},{t}^{3}}$ is a basis of ${R}_{3}[t]$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation 

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot 1+{x}_{2}\cdot t+{x}_{3}\cdot {t}^{2}+{x}_{4}\cdot {t}^{3}=0,
$$

 
is true if and only if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}={x}_{4}=0.$ So, the set is linearly independent.

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
{t}^{3}-3t+8=8\cdot 1+(-3)\cdot t+0\cdot {t}^{2}+1\cdot {t}^{3}.
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, the set is linearly independent and for any polynomial in ${R}_{3}[t],$ we get 

$$
a{t}^{3}+b{t}^{2}+ct+d=d\cdot 1+c\cdot t+b\cdot {t}^{2}+a\cdot {t}^{3}.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

questions.problem:
Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R.$

Which of the following statements are true?

- ${[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}$ is a linearly independent set in ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$
- $[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}]$ can be expressed as a linear combination of ${[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}$
- ${[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}$ is a basis of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

is true if and only if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0.$ So, the set is linearly independent.

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}]=3\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]+(-1)\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

- Statement III is false. For example, the matrix $[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 4 & -1\end{aligned}]$ can't be written as a linear combination of 

$$
{[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}
$$

since all these linear combinations result in matrices with the entry ${a}_{11}=0:$

$$
a\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]+b\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ a & 2b\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R.$

Which of the following statements are true?

- ${[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}$ is a linearly independent set in ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$
- $[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]$ can be expressed as a linear combination of ${[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}$
- ${[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}$ is a basis of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

is true if and only if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0.$ So, the set is linearly independent.

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]=2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+\frac{3}{2}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

- Statement III is false. For example, the matrix $[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]$ can't be written as a linear combination of 

$$
{[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}
$$

since all these linear combinations result in matrices with the entry ${a}_{21}=0:$

$$
a\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+b\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}a & -a \\ 0 & 2b\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements About Bases of Abstract Vector Spaces
questions.problem:
Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ be a basis of a vector space $V.$ 

Which of the following statements are true?

- ${{b}_{1},{b}_{1}-{b}_{2}}$ is a basis of $V$
- ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3},w}$ is linearly dependent
- ${{b}_{1},{b}_{3}}$ is linearly independent
questions.worked_solution:
Since $B$ is a basis, the following properties must hold:

- $B$ is a maximally linearly independent set of vectors in $V,$ and

- $B$ spans $V.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false since the vector ${b}_{3}$ can't be written as a linear combination of ${{b}_{1},{b}_{1}-{b}_{2}}.$ But then

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{3} & ={x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}({b}_{1}-{b}_{2}) \\  & =({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}){b}_{1}+(-{x}_{2}){b}_{2},\end{aligned}
$$

which would mean that $B$ is linearly dependent. This would contradict the fact that $B$ is a basis.

- Statement II is true. Since $B$ is a basis of $V,$ it is a maximally linearly independent set of vectors. This means that if we add any new vector to the set, it becomes linearly dependent.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, if ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ is linearly dependent then there exist ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}=0,
$$

where at least one of $x$'s is not zero. But then 

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+0{b}_{3}=0,
$$

which would mean that $B$ is linearly dependent. This would contradict the fact that $B$ is a basis.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

questions.problem:
Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}}$ be bases of ${R}^{2}$ and ${R}^{3},$ respectively. 

Which of the following statements are true?

- ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2},x}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$
- ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{3}$
- ${{c}_{3},{c}_{2},{c}_{1}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{3}$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $B$ and $C$ are bases, the following properties must hold:

- $B$ and $C$ are maximally linearly independent sets in ${R}^{2}$ and ${R}^{3},$ respectively, and

- $B$ spans ${R}^{2},$ while $C$ spans ${R}^{3}.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Since $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$, any vector of ${R}^{2},$ including the given vector $x,$ can be written as a linear combination of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}.$ This means that ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2},x}$ is linearly dependent and therefore, cannot be a basis.

- Statement II is false. The set ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ is not a basis of ${R}^{3}$ because the set contains vectors from another vector space.

- Statement III is true. The set ${{c}_{3},{c}_{2},{c}_{1}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{3}$ because, by reordering the vectors, we obtain the basis $C.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only".

$$

\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+(2{x}_{2}){b}_{2} & =0,\end{aligned}

- $\big\{ 0,t^2 \big\}$ is a linearly independent set in $\mathbb{R}_2[t]$

- $-5t^2$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\big\{ 0, t^2 \big\}$

- $\big\{ 0, t^2 \big\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}_2[t]$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Notice that 

$$
1 \cdot {\color{blue}0} + 0 \cdot {\color{blue}t^2} = 0,
$$

 
where the first coefficient is nonzero, so the set is linearly dependent. In general, any set that contains a zero-vector is linearly dependent.

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
-5t^2 = 0 \cdot {\color{blue}0} + (-5) \cdot {\color{blue}t^2}.
$$

- Statement III is false. Since the set is not linearly independent, it can't form a basis.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements About Bases of Abstract Vector Spaces
canonical_examples.problem:
Let $\mathcal{B}= \left\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3} \right\}$ be a basis of a vector space $V.$ 

Which of the following statements are true?

- $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2},- \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_3}+\mathbf{b_1} \right\}$ is a basis of $V$

- $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3}, \mathbf{0}  \right\}$ spans $V$

- $\left\{  -\mathbf{b_2}, 3\mathbf{b_1}\right\}$ is linearly dependent
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis, the following properties must hold:

- $\mathcal{B}$ is a maximally linearly independent set of vectors in $V,$ and

- $\mathcal{B}$ spans $V.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{2}+{x}_{2}(-{b}_{1})+{x}_{3}({b}_{3}+{b}_{1}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

is equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{2}+({x}_{3}-{x}_{2}){b}_{1}+{x}_{3}{b}_{3} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, since $\left\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3} \right\}$ is linearly independent, gives
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066905/assets/44e05962671a66862ed2fb7a4bc3fc2f859d3a66c56274b869724ee47f6c6414.png)
Also, $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2},- \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_3}+\mathbf{b_1} \right\}$ spans $V$ since any linear combination of vectors from $\mathcal{B}$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2},- \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_3}+\mathbf{b_1} \right\}\mathbin{:}$

$$
x_1\mathbf{b}_1+x_2\mathbf{b}_2+x_3\mathbf{b}_3
=
x_2\mathbf{b}_2+(x_3-x_1)(-\mathbf{b}_1)+x_3 (\mathbf{b_3}+\mathbf{b_1})
$$

- Statement II is false. In order for $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3}, \mathbf{0}  \right\}$ to span $V,$ every element of $\mathcal{B}$ must be able to be expressed as a linear combination of elements of $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3}, \mathbf{0}  \right\}.$ But the vector $\mathbf{b}_1 \in \mathcal{B}$ can't be written as a linear combination of the elements of $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3}, \mathbf{0}  \right\}.$

- Statement III is false. If $\left\{  -\mathbf{b_2}, 3\mathbf{b_1}\right\}$ is linearly dependent then there exist $x_1$ and $x_2$ not both zero such that

$$
x_1(-\mathbf{b_2}) + x_2(3\mathbf{b_1}) = \mathbf{0}.
$$

Then, we would have

$$
(3x_2) \cdot \mathbf{b_1} + (-x_1) \cdot \mathbf{b_2} + 0 \cdot \mathbf{b}_3= \mathbf{0}.
$$

But this would mean that $\mathcal{B} = \left\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3} \right\}$ is linearly dependent, which contradicts the fact that $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis of $V.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."
